chapter_theme: The women and people of the city praise Civakan and argue for tapas; he worships the Jina in his temple with hymns and an endowment, then sits among kings and pays out his debts of land, rule and wealth to brother, friends, nurses, kin and uncle, and builds a golden memorial for the friend who saved him.

cast.role: the hero, now victor and king
the women of the city who praise Civakan
the people of the city, here arguing for tapas
kings related to Civakan by marriage
king of Videham, Civakan's maternal uncle
the nurses who brought up Civakan

2551.reading: The women of the city say that the woman who bore the prince has by her great austerity lit up the whole world, and that the greatest vow among women must be Sunandai's, whose chastity never broke.
2551.nuance: The verse echoes the street talk in 465, where the people ask what penance Civakan's mother did. Whether the first woman (the one who bore him) and Sunandai (who raised him) are one or two is not settled by the words, so the praise may belong to either.

claims.claim: a mother's great austerity shows in the glory of her son
the greatest vow among women is a chaste wife's unbroken steadfastness

2552.reading: The women say that those women who press against him, crushing their sandalled breasts and garlands as they cling, are not truly fortunate women but false ones, bearing hair, breasts, pearls and garlands only to waste away.
2552.nuance: It is unclear whether the speakers mock rival women or pity them; the sense of the last two lines (போந்த அந்நங்கைமார்கள் பொய்ந்நங்கைமார்கள்) turns on that.

2553.reading: The women urge one another to drink in his beauty, their wide dark eyes cupped like palms, each taking her fill so that none is left out.
2553.nuance: The third line sets a vine-woman whose whole body became eyes against the sharing; the exact turn of the thought is hard to fix.

2554.reading: The women say that from the day he left the breast, as a lion tears the tusks from the head of a fallen elephant, he slew his foes the moment he took up the bow, and that the world may now sleep in the shade of his moon-bright umbrella.

2555.reading: They say that anyone who sees how he was born in this city's burning ground, how he grew up as a matchless merchant's son, and how kings have come to worship him must ask why one should live heedless instead of doing penance.
2555.nuance: Civakan's rise from the burning ground (304) is made here into an argument for tapas, in the epic's own mouth, before the last ilampakam where he does take it up. The subject of the last line (the city folk, or each hearer, or Civakan himself) is not fixed by the verse.

claims.claim: a life that has turned as fortune turns should lead one to take up penance and not live heedless

2556.reading: The speakers say that, however a man crosses roaring seas and mountains and suffers sickness, wealth does not come without fortune's favour, while it may come home to those who go not a cubit; so let tapas be taken up with effort.
2556.nuance: The Tamil of lines 3 and 4 (the words after ஒருமுழமும் சேறலிலரேனும்) is hard, and the verse's speaker is taken from the neighbouring verses; read it as a loose argument from fortune to tapas.

claims.claim: gain of wealth depends on fortune, not on travel and toil
tapas should be practised in preference to toil for wealth

2557.reading: They say that one strong in tapas takes no harm even from poison and escapes even from between a mighty elephant's tusks, whereas once tapas is spent no hiding in fear saves; so the fearless, with dharma as their refuge, are those rich in tapas.
2557.nuance: The words ஆணில்லை and களைகண் are rare, and both the grammar of line 2 and the sense of the closing phrase are read from the whole stanza.

claims.claim: tapas protects from poison and the tusker, and when it is spent no flight saves
dharma itself is the refuge of the fearless who are strong in tapas

2558.reading: Passing through the city amid its praise, the lord of the shore goes to the temple of the king of the flowering pindi tree, which the verse sets round with pearl-bearing conches and screwpine on the sea's edge.
2558.nuance: The one who goes is called கடற்சேர்ப்பன் (lord of the shore), an unusual title for Civakan; he is taken as Civakan because the next verses show him worship and endow the temple. The pindi (asoka) tree is the Jina's tree.
2558.event: Civakan goes in procession to the Jina's temple.

2559.reading: In the flowery grove, where peacocks dance, swans cry and koels call, he puts aside his weapons and arrives at the golden temple of the one with the twisted, resounding anklet.
2559.nuance: The verse does not say why he lays down arms; the step before the shrine reads as a mark of reverence.
2559.event: Civakan sets aside his guard and reaches the golden temple.

2560.reading: Circling the gem-doored shrine thick with aloe smoke, the king of kings says that he has been born, will not be born again, and has found the one who is not born; then bows, shakes his head in praise and worships with his hands.
2560.nuance: The claim is made by the hero in worship and rests on reaching the unborn one; the verse does not say the Jina acts to free him.
2560.event: Civakan circles the Jina's shrine and worships, declaring that his births end.

claims.claim: one who comes to the feet of the unborn one is not born again

2561.reading: They hymn the one with the sacred mark on his chest and the three-umbrella crest, father of the sages who bear the rare scripture, and say they worship his fire-bright lotus feet.
2561.nuance: The stanza is built by repeating its second line's words in the third (as 2562 and 2563 do), a hymn form and not a text fault; the 'we' (தொழுதும்) leaves it open whether Civakan sings alone or with his company.

claims.claim: the Jina is the father of the sages who hold the rare scripture

2562.reading: They hymn the god who knows the world, of fearful might, whose path is unequalled in its moon-bright ornament, and worship his lotus feet.
2562.nuance: Built like 2561, with the second line's words repeated in the third.

claims.claim: the Jina knows the whole world and his way has no equal

2563.reading: They hymn the one who understood without fault, the wheel that removes stain, the lord of merit who set bounds to the senses, and worship his fragrant lotus feet.
2563.nuance: Built like 2561, with the second line's words repeated in the third.

claims.claim: the Jina, stainless and master of the senses, is the first of merit

2564.reading: Civakan lays at the feet of the one who walked on the red lotus an endowment of four crore, a hundred old towns, rutting tuskers and a hundred flagged chariots, that the lamp which never fails may be kept.
2564.nuance: The opening of line 2 (நொந்தார்க் கடந்தான் கொடுத்தான்) can be read as a gift to the afflicted or as a clause about the foe-conqueror; and 'புறம்' for the lamp is read as its endowment.
2564.event: Civakan endows the Jina's temple with gold, towns, elephants and chariots.

2565.reading: He offers garlands that never fade, of gems, gold, pearl and coral, hung so that they fall like streams, then the foe-conqueror circles the shrine and goes on to his own place.
2565.event: Civakan offers garlands, circles the shrine and goes on.

2566.reading: Seated on a couch of gems made from the right tusks of the elephants his enemies rode, the lord of the earth sits raised among the kings, praised by the goddess of learning and joined to faultless Fortune.
2566.nuance: The couch turns the defeated kings' own elephants into his seat.
2566.event: Civakan sits among the kings on a couch made of the enemy's elephant tusks.

2567.reading: While the world rises to ask what penance the man must have done, he gives a feast of rule and a share of land to the one of famed repute, and gives the Chittiratevi title to the mother who toiled to raise him.
2567.nuance: The world's cry 'what penance did he do!' recalls the Kural's phrase for a son's repayment to his father (kural:70), but with different words; the verse does not name who receives the feast or which mother is meant (Sunandai is the nurse named in 2551).
2567.event: Civakan gives land and rule to the famed one and the queen's title to the mother who raised him.

claims.claim: a son repays the one who raised him in rank and land

2568.reading: At the kings' praise he installs his younger brother as the heir, calls him his own, joins him to kings' daughters and gives him a rich land, bidding him live as he pleases.
2568.nuance: The title இளவுடையான் is read as heir or the younger one; the brother is Nandattan only by inference from the story.
2568.event: Civakan sets up his younger brother with a kingdom and royal brides.

2569.reading: The king gives his dear friends, who suffered long with him, a rule and treasure unmatched on earth, with gem ring, gold crest and garland, and bids them live.
2569.event: Civakan gives his companions treasure and a country.

2570.reading: He calls the nurses who reared him, honours their kin, and to the amazement of the hearers gives five villages and a thousand days of produce with the right to levy dues, and the king breathes easy.
2570.nuance: The last two lines turn on இறுப்புத் தண்டக் கொள; the grant is read as the right to collect dues.
2570.event: Civakan rewards the nurses and their families with villages and dues.

2571.reading: To the kings of his marriage-kin, who clung to him in devotion like the young held by a monkey and had trained with him in arms, he gives gold chariots, wealth, gem-wrought horse chariots, sea-going horses and rutting elephants.
2571.event: Civakan gives chariots, horses and elephants to his kinsmen kings.

2572.reading: Having picked out all that belonged to Kattiyangaran, the wicked son of lion-like strength, he gives it to his uncle Govindan, king of fine chariots, and stays like an inexhaustible cow even to the guardian of the world.
2572.event: Civakan gives the usurper's goods to his uncle Govindan.

2573.reading: For the friend who lifted a great trouble from him he makes a place, has his likeness wrought in gold and set up so that the city and the land praise it, and himself has the friend's whole story made into a dance.
2573.nuance: The first line reads corrupt (நீக்கிப் யாய). The friend is taken as Sudanjanan, the god who was once the dog Civakan helped (945) and who carried him from trouble, but the verse never names him.
2573.event: Civakan sets up a golden image and a dance of his friend's story.

claims.claim: a good done in distress is owed a lasting public memorial

2574.reading: Thinking of the strength of his sharp spear, he decks with honey-dripping garlands the fine place where he used to play, sets a golden seat there, and makes five villages its surround.
2574.nuance: The noun ஆலை is read as a hall or workplace and not a mill, and what the place was is not fixed by this verse.
2574.event: Civakan adorns the place of his old play and endows it with five villages.

links.note: The people of Govindai's ilampakam said that the good mother who bore the lord must have done great penance and asked on which hill she did it; here the women of the city again set a mother's penance behind the son's glory, and name Sunandai as the great vower.
links.teaches: The street's guess that a hero's greatness is a mother's earned penance is first a wonder at his youth and is now a verdict on his rule, and the woman named for it changes from the one who bore him to the one who raised him.

links.note: At the birth in the burning ground the child shone like the sun from the sea, gem lamps drove off the dark and the place's deities bowed; the people now call up that same birthplace beside his rise as a merchant's son and kings' lord.
links.teaches: The burning-ground birth that was a picture of desolation becomes the first term of a turn of fortune that the epic offers as a reason to take up tapas.

links.note: Kattiyangaran took the land by a gift of law that was no true gift (வஞ்சம்) and gathered its wealth; Civakan now picks out all that belonged to him and gives it to Govindan, the uncle who stood with him.
links.teaches: The usurper's hoard is not destroyed but passes to the kin he had wronged, so the plot closes the fraud of 240 by moving the goods, not by punishing anything beyond the man.

links.note: Civakan whispered the five mantras into the dying dog's ear, seed that frees one of former karma, and the dog became a yaksha; the friend whose story he now has danced and whose golden image he sets up is, if the friend is that god, the debt repaid for that mercy.
links.teaches: A kindness to a dying animal is paid back in a rescue and then in the first public memorial the epic records, so the charity of 945 outlasts the dog's death in the city's own ritual.

links.note: The world asks 'what penance must he have done' and the king repays the one who reared him with a queen's title; the couplet makes that very kind of question the repayment a son owes his father.
links.teaches: The couplet's repayment is a sentence the world speaks; the epic adds a repayment made in rank and land and paid to the nurse, so the debt to one who raised a child need not stay in words and is not only the father's.

gains.a: the couplet's frame that the world's astonished 'what penance did he do' is itself the son's gift, which the verse leaves as bare talk
gains.b: a case where the debt is paid in rank, land and the title of queen, and to a rearing mother, which the couplet's wish for a father's good name never reaches

links.note: Wealth does not come across seas and mountains without fortune, and may come home to those who go not a cubit; the couplet says what is not one's own will not stay and what is will not leave.
links.teaches: The epic draws the practical conclusion the couplet leaves unsaid: if wealth is the share fortune gives, the effort spent seeking it is better spent on tapas.

gains.a: the couplet's flat rule about fate that grounds why effort for wealth is not the safe course
gains.b: a seafaring merchant's world of crossings and sickness, which the couplet gives no instance of, and a use for the rule in recommending tapas

links.note: Poison, hiding and the elephant's tusks are the dangers the strong in tapas escape; the couplet says austerity's power lets one even leap past Death.
links.teaches: The Kural states the power of tapas at its limit and the epic lists the particular harms it turns aside, and adds that when tapas is spent no flight saves.

gains.a: the couplet's claim that tapas power reaches even to Death, beyond poison and tusks
gains.b: named perils (poison, the tusker) and the warning that spent tapas leaves no hiding place, which the couplet's bare 'even leaping past death' lacks

links.note: Civakan lays his endowment at the feet of the one who walked on the red lotus; the Kural's opening couplets name the one who walked on the flower and promise long life to those who reach his feet.
links.teaches: The epic names the lotus and puts a temple and a gift at the feet, filling in the figure the couplet leaves open, so it shows one tradition's reading of the lotus-walker as the Jina's temple god.

gains.a: the couplet's idea that to reach the lotus-walker's feet is the aim of the faithful and not only a courtesy
gains.b: a worshipper's act of endowing the feet with lamp, towns and chariots, and a reader who takes the lotus-walker as the Jina, which the couplet does not say

links.note: Civakan raises a golden image and a dance to the friend who wiped away his trouble, and that friend was once a dog who changed birth; the couplet says the friendship of those who wiped away sorrow is remembered for seven births.
links.teaches: The Kural's memory across births becomes a literal chain from dog to god, and the epic makes the memory public and material in image and dance where the couplet leaves it in the heart.

gains.a: the couplet's measure that a rescue is owed memory beyond one life, which explains why a gold image is not too much
gains.b: a case where the friendship does cross births and is kept up in public ritual, which the couplet has only as a promise

links.note: The people see the hero's birth in the burning ground, rearing as a merchant's son and the kings' worship and ask why one should not do tapas; the quatrain has the best renounce home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength because none lasts.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar argues renunciation from the failing of goods in general, and the epic argues it from one life in which a single man has held every state, so the argument rests on a case the hearers have seen.

gains.a: the quatrain's list of what fails (home, youth, wealth, strength) as the reason that makes tapas the sensible answer to his rise
gains.b: a named life that has lived through desolation, rearing and kingship, which the quatrain's list of goods never shows in one person

links.note: Civakan says he will not be born again, having found the unborn one; Tirumular says that after he renounced and saw the light the lord of the gods set him here so that he would not die and be born again.
links.teaches: Both end births by reaching a lord who is not born, but the Saiva verse makes the lord the one who sets the seeker free while the epic verse puts the claim in the worshipper's mouth and does not say the Jina acts.

gains.a: the Saiva verse's mechanism, a lord who sets the seeker beyond birth, which Civakan's cry of certainty lacks
gains.b: a parallel from a worshipper of the unborn Jina who rests his claim on reaching the feet, which shows how the end-of-birth language is shared and the cause differs

source_issues: 2573 line 1 reads corrupt: நீக்கிப் யாய is short and the word பயாய is not a word as printed.
2551-2554, 2558-2560, 2567-2572 and 2573-2574 print as 8 half-lines joined into 4 (the tool's repair).
2561-2563 repeat the second line's words in the third; this is the stanza form, not doubling.
